Specifically, we propose a weighted average mechanism in SO(3) based on the angle-axis representation method. Our main idea is to generate multiple trajectories by considering different local constraints at different basepoints. Then these multiple trajectories are fused to generate a smooth trajectory by our proposed weighted average mechanism, achieving the goal to incorporate multiple local constraints simultaneously. Compared with existing solution, ours can address the distortion issue and make the off-theshelf Euclidean learning algorithm be re-applicable in non-Euclidean space. Simulation and Experimental evaluations validate that our solution can not only adapt orientations towards arbitrary desired via-points and cope with angular acceleration constraints, but also incorporate multiple local constraints simultaneously to achieve extra benefits, e.g., achieving smaller acceleration costs.

signals.title: A Shared-Autonomy Construction Robotic System for Overhead Works
signals.summary: arXiv:2511.09695v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the ongoing development of a robotic system for overhead work such as ceiling drilling. The hardware platform comprises a mobile base with a two-stage lift, on which a bimanual torso is mounted with a custom-designed drilling end effector and RGB-D cameras. To support teleoperation in dynamic environments with limited visibility, we use Gaussian splatting for online 3D reconstruction and introduce motion parameters to model moving objects. For safe operation around dynamic obstacles, we developed a neural configuration-space barrier approach for planning and control. Initial feasibility studies demonstrate the capability of the hardware in drilling, bolting, and anchoring, and the software in safe teleoperation in a dynamic environment. Experiment videos and results are available at https://kmk9846.github.io/Construction-Robot/

signals.title: Latent Reasoning VLA: Latent Thinking and Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2602.01166v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models benefit from chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but existing approaches incur high inference overhead and rely on discrete reasoning representations that mismatch continuous perception and control. We propose Latent Reasoning VLA (LaRA-VLA), a unified VLA framework that internalizes multi-modal CoT reasoning into continuous latent representations for embodied action. LaRA-VLA performs unified reasoning and prediction in latent space, eliminating explicit CoT generation at inference time and enabling efficient, action-oriented control. To realize latent embodied reasoning, we introduce a curriculum-based training paradigm that progressively transitions from explicit textual and visual CoT supervision to latent reasoning, and finally adapts latent reasoning dynamics to condition action generation. We construct two structured CoT datasets and evaluate LaRA-VLA on both simulation benchmarks and long-horizon real-robot manipulation tasks. Experimental results show that LaRA-VLA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art VLA methods while reducing inference latency by up to 90\% compared to explicit CoT-based approaches, demonstrating latent reasoning as an effective and efficient paradigm for real-time embodied control. Project Page: https://loveju1y.github.io/Latent-Reasoning-VLA/

signals.title: UNILARN: Latent Action Pretraining with Dedicated RGB, Depth, and Unified RGB-Depth Supervision
signals.summary: arXiv:2602.20231v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Depth provides critical geometric supervision for robot manipulation, yet existing depth-aware policies typically inject it through fused representations or auxiliary objectives, leaving its role in action learning implicit. We introduce UNILARN, a latent-action pretraining framework that explicitly preserves three complementary supervisory targets from RGB-D transitions: RGB-specific, depth-specific, and unified latent actions. RGB and depth transition embeddings are first discretized through a shared codebook, then fused and re-quantized through a separate unified codebook, preserving modality-specific dynamics while modeling their shared action semantics. These three latent-action targets provide separate pseudo-action supervision during VLA pretraining, avoiding both inconsistent independent learning and premature multimodal fusion without requiring robot action labels. The pretrained VLA is subsequently fine-tuned on executable actions and requires only RGB observations and language instructions at inference. Experiments in simulation and the real-world show improvements over RGB-based latent-action pretraining, particularly on geometry-sensitive manipulation tasks.

signals.title: SG-DOR: Learning Scene Graphs with Direction-Conditioned Occlusion Reasoning for Pepper Plants
signals.summary: arXiv:2603.06512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robotic harvesting in dense crop canopies requires effective interventions that depend not only on geometry, but also on explicit, direction-conditioned relations identifying which organs obstruct a target fruit. We present SG-DOR (Scene Graphs with Direction-Conditioned Occlusion Reasoning), a relational framework that, given instance-segmented organ point clouds, infers a scene graph encoding physical attachments and direction-conditioned occlusion. We introduce an \emph{occlusion ranking} task for retrieving and ranking candidate leaves for a target fruit and approach direction, and propose a direction-aware graph neural architecture with per-fruit leaf-set attention and union-level aggregation. Experiments on a multi-plant synthetic pepper dataset show improved occlusion prediction (F1=0.73, NDCG@3=0.85) and attachment inference (edge F1=0.83) over strong ablations, yielding a structured relational signal for downstream intervention planning.

signals.title: Perception-Aware Multi-UAV Implicit Coordination in the Wild
signals.summary: arXiv:2603.08379v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a perception-aware 3D navigation system for decentralized multi-robot coordination in cluttered environments, such as forests with dense canopy cover where GNSS is unavailable. Our novel perception-aware approach computes collision-free motion toward a goal region while accounting for the limited field of view of the sensor, and is combined with a replanner to guide multiple robots to their goal. The system relies on an onboard anisotropic 3D LiDAR, used for localization, mapping, and detection of obstacles and neighboring robots. Decentralized coordination among the robots emerges as a byproduct of local interactions and common rules, so no explicit communication is required. The system is evaluated through extensive single and multi-robot simulations across diverse scenarios and validated in multiple real-world field experiments.

signals.title: RankFormer: A Propose-then-Select Transformer for Multi-Agent Multimodal Trajectory Prediction
signals.summary: arXiv:2604.07126v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting traffic agent trajectories plays an important role in autonomous driving, traffic operations, transportation safety analysis, etc. Although many deep learning algorithms are devised to predict future agent trajectories, the trajectory prediction problem is still challenging due to the complexity of decision-making process, interactions with surrounding vehicles, and the existence of multiple possible intentions for the traveling agents even under similar scenarios. Most existing methods are limited by the requirement of graph structures (e.g., Graph Neural Network) or the requirement of manually labeled intentions. In this study, we propose a pure Transformer-based deep learning model for multi-modal trajectory prediction considering temporal dependencies and agent-agent spatial interactions. After encoding the historical trajectories, two parallel decoders are employed to generate trajectories and probabilities on separate decoder tracks. The model is evaluated on two real-world datasets, one highway dataset and the other pedestrian dataset with solid performance. One important insight is that following a ``propose-then-select'' strategy, the agent-agent spatial interactions are only considered for probability estimation instead of trajectory generation. In summary, the proposed model provides a potential direction to design more robust and effective multi-modal trajectory prediction models.

signals.title: Self-Supervised Online Robot-Agnostic Traversability Estimation for Open-World Environments
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.28442v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-supervised online traversability estimation enables robots to continuously learn from unlabeled open-world experiences and adapt their navigation behavior toward safe and efficient trajectories. Existing approaches either rely on handcrafted proprioceptive traversability scores, limiting robot-agnosticism, or cluster prior data, preventing online learning. Moreover, many continual learning methods incur substantial memory and computational costs, hindering onboard deployment. We introduce COTRATE, an online learning framework for continuous traversability estimation from multimodal, unlabeled robot experience. Our method first infers robust traversability scores using a robot-agnostic, learning-based online terrain assessment module operating on proprioceptiveand inertial signals. These scores then supervise a visual traversability network through a novel alignment loss that associates visual embeddings with online terrain assessments. To mitigate forgetting during continual learning with minimal overhead, we propose a diversity-aware feature selection strategythat preserves performance using a compact replay memory. We further show that the learned traversability representation supports knowledge transfer across different robot platforms with different locomotion kinematics. We evaluate COTRATE on a dataset of $\approx$ 50,000 images collected with two robotic platforms across 11 outdoor terrains, and benchmark it on navigation tasks in three representative outdoor environments. We make the dataset, code, and trained models publicly available.

signals.title: 3DVLA: Enhancing Vision-Language-Action Models via 3D Spatial and Instance Understanding
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.29416v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation, yet they suffer from a critical limitation: a lack of 3D scene understanding. This deficiency manifests as three intertwined challenges: weak extraction of 3D spatial positions without enforcing multi-view consistency, inadequate 3D instance understanding, and fragile reasoning under occlusion. Although mature 3D perception methods exist, their direct integration into VLA pipelines is hindered by architectural incompatibility and by heavy reliance on costly instance-level annotations. To address these challenges, we propose 3DVLA, a framework compatible with existing VLA models, which introduces 3D understanding without requiring extra manual labels or discarding VLM priors. Specifically, 3DVLA tackles the three challenges through: (1) pervasive 3D feature encoding with explicit multi-view consistency constraints across all modalities and a Spatially-Conditioned Geometry Aggregation method, (2) an object-centric 3D instance module with high-level instance tokens for 3D instance awareness, and (3) a masked self-supervised 3D encoding branch that retains its predictor for visual token completion to handle occlusions. We integrate 3DVLA with multiple VLA baselines and evaluate on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world settings. Results show consistent and significant gains in manipulation performance, validating both the effectiveness and plug-and-play compatibility of our approach.

signals.title: DriveAnchor: Progressive Anchor-based Flow Learning for Autonomous Driving Planning
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.00519v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous-driving planners must generate route- and maneuver-compliant trajectories under a limited decoder-call budget while adapting offline to black-box static-collision feedback. We propose DriveAnchor, a three-stage framework built around a shared vocabulary of recorded trajectories and a continuous trajectory interface. The vocabulary supports flow-matching (FM) residual learning, Energy Field (EF) corridor-conditioned initialization, and anchor-guided zeroth-order reward fine-tuning. The reward update operates in trajectory space without policy likelihoods or reward gradients, enabling offline adaptation of a deterministic decoder. On sampled nuPlan scenarios, EF guidance and reward fine-tuning each improve the mean closed-loop score. On the same cases, the official pretrained Diffusion Planner scores higher with our reward update than with supervised fine-tuning. We further integrate the trajectory generator into a real vehicle's planning pipeline and demonstrate its operation on urban roads. On 10,000 held-out internal scenarios, under the original non-EF prior and a fixed two-call FM budget, reward fine-tuning reduces short- and long-horizon static candidate collision rates from 27.22% and 56.54% to 2.94% and 7.15%, respectively, and improves 8-s best-of-set minADE from 2.27 to 1.34 m. In a separate junction diagnostic on checkpoints before Stage 3, one and two EF calls raise corridor-guidance satisfaction from 22.10% to 74.13% and 87.92%, respectively. Additional ablations support the vocabulary size and the anchor-guided sampling configuration. On NVIDIA Drive Orin, two EF calls and two FM calls take 2.06 ms per scene on average. Code and deployment videos are available on the project page: https://drivean

signals.title: Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filtering for Data-Efficient Joint Tracking and Classification
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.02767v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kalman filtering performance is highly sensitive to model mismatch and noise covariance tuning. Classical adaptive filtering methods address these issues by estimating model parameters or noise covariances from measurement data but rely on a predefined model structure. Learning-based methods provide greater flexibility but typically require large supervised datasets and often lack well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. This article proposes a self-supervised Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filter (HAKF) that learns time-varying corrections to the system dynamics and process-noise covariance directly from measurements while jointly estimating the measurement-noise covariance. Because these corrections are learned from measurements alone, we analyze the structural identifiability of the corresponding time-invariant parameterizations. For a constant-velocity model with position-only measurements, an unrestricted process-noise covariance is not identifiable even when the dynamics are known, whereas a physically structured parameterization that couples the dynamics and process covariance is jointly identifiable with the measurement-noise covariance. This analysis motivates a structured HAKF variant, compared with a flexible variant that adapts the dynamics and process covariance independently. The innovation likelihood of HAKF also enables model classification through generalized Bayesian inference. In Isaac Lab simulations, the structured HAKF improves tracking accuracy over a fitted Kalman filter across all training-set sizes. When training data are limited, its advantage over the flexible variant is largest, and it outperforms a supervised recurrent neural network in both tracking and classification. On recorded DPJAIT flight tra

signals.title: OASIS: From Simulation Data Collection to Real-World Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.08548v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent progress in robot manipulation has been largely driven by learning from large-scale demonstrations. For humanoid robot loco-manipulation tasks, however, existing data sources force an unsatisfying tradeoff between trajectory quality and scalability. Real-world teleoperation provides the highest-quality trajectories but requires dedicated physical space and time-consuming scene resets. Simulation offers an alternative way out of this dilemma: it can produce clean, embodiment-aligned data at scale without any physical hardware. In this paper, we propose OASIS, a simulation-data-driven framework for humanoid loco-manipulation. OASIS automatically reconstructs realistic object assets from real-world images using a 3D generative model. Based on these assets, trajectories are first collected through teleoperation in simulation, and then augmented under diverse domain randomizations in a post-processing stage. With the resulting simulation data, we further design a hierarchical visuomotor policy for humanoid loco-manipulation. Extensive experiments on the real humanoid robot show that, under zero-shot deployment, the policy trained on our simulation data achieves higher success rates on most tasks than that trained on real-robot teleoperation data, owing largely to the broad lighting and environmental variations covered by our simulation rendering, which real-robot data fails to capture. The project page is available at https://oasis-humanoid.github.io/.

signals.title: YUBI: Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation at Scale
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.10244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface (YUBI), a finger-aligned gripper designed to enable intuitive, ergonomic, and scalable data collection for bimanual dexterous manipulation. While handheld data collection systems such as Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enable affordable data collection, their bulky pistol-grip designs can pose ergonomic and usability challenges for fine-grained, dexterous manipulation tasks. To address this, YUBI presents a distinct design principle: yielding, finger-driven actuation that directly maps human finger movements to gripper jaw motion. Using the YUBI devices, we set up a data collection system with integrated VR-based 6 DoF tracking of the gripper, ensuring high-fidelity trajectory data acquisition. We curate a UMI-based dataset of unprecedented scale: 8,434 hours across 1.20M episodes and 119 tasks. Experiments show that YUBI offers advantages over the UMI gripper in versatility for complex bimanual tasks, dexterity, and operational efficiency. A single policy trained on the YUBI dataset transfers across multiple bimanual robots (UR, Franka, and ELEY) simply by mounting the gripper on each platform, confirming that the collected data are directly executable as policy supervision. We release the gripper hardware, data-collection software, and dataset as one integrated stack, offering the open community a reproducible path to large-scale data acquisition for advancing robotic foundation models.

signals.title: Stubborn: A Streamlined and Unified Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robust Motion Tracking and Fall Recovery for Humanoids
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.12814v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent reinforcement learning approaches have shown great promise in improving humanoid motion tracking performance and achieving fall recovery under disturbances. However, most existing works treat motion tracking and fall recovery as different tasks and require multi-stage training with specialized recovery rewards and/or separate recovery policies. Moreover, existing reinforcement learning-based methods often terminate training episodes immediately after severe tracking failures, limiting recovery-oriented exploration in unstable or fallen states. To address the above issues, we propose Stubborn, a streamlined and unified reinforcement learning framework to achieve robust humanoid motion tracking and fall recovery. Specifically, Stubborn uses an asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture and consists of three major components. First, a yaw-aligned tracking representation is adopted to reduce sensitivity to global drift and heading disturbances while preserving gravity-related balance information. Second, we introduce a Bernoulli-based probabilistic termination mechanism that enables the policy to encourage exploration of fall-recovery behaviors under varying failure modes. Third, we propose a probabilistic termination and tracking-error-driven strategy that dynamically reshapes the sampling distribution based on tracking performance, increasing the training efficiency for difficult motion segments and unstable states. Extensive comparisons with SOTA methods and ablation studies show that Stubborn achieved competitive performance and avoided the reward-hacking tendency of baseline methods, and the proposed probabilistic termination mechanism and adaptive sampling strategy contributed to the performance and robustness gains

signals.title: $\lambda$-Reachability: Geometric-Horizon Safety Bellman Equations for Humanoid Safety
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.16022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce $\lambda$-Reachability, a scalable approach to Hamilton--Jacobi safety analysis for high-dimensional robotic systems. Unlike prior discounted formulations that rely on fixed one-step Bellman updates, $\lambda$-Reachability employs a stochastic multi-step estimator of the safety value, using a geometrically distributed rollout horizon together with a randomly absorbed terminal. Conceptually analogous to TD($\lambda$), $\lambda$-Reachability interpolates between local self-consistency updates and long-horizon max-over-trajectory safety targets via an interpretable horizon-control parameter. Unlike TD($\lambda$), where the terminal value is always incorporated in learning targets, the terminal safety value in $\lambda$-Reachability is only used at a probability controlled by parameter $\delta$. We formally show that for $\delta<1$, the update induces a contraction mapping that allows temporal-difference learning; as $\lambda \to 1$, the estimator recovers the undiscounted reachability objective. We apply $\lambda$-Reachability to high-dimensional safety learning problems with both simulated and real humanoid robots under balance and collision avoidance constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that $\lambda$-Reachability significantly improves both safe-set boundary classification and safety margin estimation compared to single-step temporal-difference baselines.

signals.title: Learning from Failure: Robot Self-Improvement via Human Videos
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.21406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning from deployment experience is essential for robots to improve their performance in the real world. A robot should be able to learn from failed executions, but these do not reveal which actions would have succeeded, and obtaining corrections from human experts requires costly monitoring and intervention. Human videos offer a rich source of interaction experience, showing how actions change the environment and lead to task completion. To turn this experience into corrective supervision, we introduce Dynamics-Guided Action Correction (DGAC), which uses dynamics and value models pretrained on human videos to construct alternative actions at failed states and evaluate their outcomes without executing each candidate. We evaluate our method on seven real-world manipulation tasks across two robot embodiments and demonstrate that it improves the average success rate from 40% to 81%, requiring no expert corrections during self-improvement. We further show that generated corrections enable recovery from failed executions and provide more effective training targets than imagined policy rollouts using the same models and data. Finally, we demonstrate that human-video dynamics and value models provide effective corrective supervision for policies pretrained on either human or robot data, suggesting that human videos benefit robot learning in addition to policy initialization.

signals.title: PAC-ACT: Post-training Actor-Critic for Action Chunking Transformers
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.09590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Precision industrial contact manipulation requires reliable robot policies under pose perturbations and contact-force constraints. Vision-language-action models offer broad generalization but often introduce high inference latency and GPU-memory cost, while vision-action chunking policies are more suitable for real-time industrial control. However, these policies are usually trained by behavior cloning and suffer from distribution shift in contact-rich tasks. This paper proposes PAC-ACT, a reinforcement-learning post-training framework for pretrained Action Chunking Transformer policies. PAC-ACT reformulates policy optimization at the chunk level, constructs an ACT-transferred actor-critic architecture, and introduces a hybrid behavior-prior constraint to preserve the pretrained action distribution during online fine-tuning. Experiments on industrial precision-contact benchmarks show that PAC-ACT improves task success, contact stability, and force safety while retaining low latency and low GPU-memory usage. On the Contour task, PAC-ACT significantly reduces peak contact force and decreases the proportion of force readings above 60 N by 46 times. Sparse-reward ablations further show that the proposed behavior-prior constraint enables effective exploration under randomized initial poses.

signals.title: Video2Track: Steerable Adversarial Scenario Generation from Real-World Interaction Videos to Proving Grounds for Automated Driving System Testing
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.11592v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physical proving-ground testing enables controlled and repeatable validation of automated driving systems (ADSs). However, existing approaches often rely on manually designed reference routes and scripted vehicle behaviors, limiting deployment efficiency, real-world interaction reproduction, and interaction risk steerability. To address these limitations, we propose Video2Track, a framework that converts real-world driving videos into steerable adversarial scenarios for proving-ground testing. Video2Track extracts interaction semantics using a vision-language model, retrieves compatible maneuver pairs on the target road network, and generates reference trajectories through interaction-guided diffusion. Game-based online refinement adjusts background vehicle (BV) trajectories based on real-time feedback from the vehicle under test (VUT) to regulate interaction risk toward a prescribed anticipated post-encroachment time (APET). Video2Track achieved an interaction consistency rate of 82.1\% and a scenario generation success rate of 78.6\%. In proving-ground tests, the mean minimum APET was within 0.5~s of each of the four target values. Video2Track also achieved lower mean minimum APET values than the evaluated baselines in both cut-in and unprotected left-turn scenarios. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring real-world driving interactions to executable proving-ground scenarios, enabling faithful interaction reproduction and steerable adversarial testing on an Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled 5G cloud-controlled platform.

signals.title: WM-VS: Progress-Aligned World Models for Closed-Loop Visual Servoing
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.20892v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Closed-loop visual servoing requires predictions that indicate whether an action reduces task error, not only whether the action is plausible. We call this gap the prediction-control mismatch and introduce WM-VS, a target-centric progress-aligned world-model framework for closed-loop visual servoing. Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a signed four-dimensional servo coordinate for translation, scale, and in-plane rotation. Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy with action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts that favor error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, without online trajectory optimization. On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, WM-VS reaches a corner RMSE no larger than 10 percent of its initial value in 30/30 trials and retains this criterion at the final valid frame in 25/30 (83.33 percent). Removing future-error alignment reduces retention to 26.67 percent. The learned progress signal agrees with an external AprilTag corner error not used for training or control (mean Spearman rho = 0.8778). Without retraining, two unseen 3D targets achieve translation-error reductions of 86.48 percent and 90.27 percent and rotation-error reductions of 70.01 percent and 65.70 percent. These results link progress-aligned action consequences to repeated closed-loop correction and transfer. Code and data will be released as open source.

signals.title: CHOREO: From Single Skill to Continuous Humanoid Execution
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.22274v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Motion data, RL policies, and generative models give humanoids thousands of skills, and the best general trackers execute nearly all of them alone. Chained to follow a language instruction, the skills fail far more often: in simulation, even the best of eight trackers reaches only 84.9\% sequence success, and their average is 48.9\%. This is because validating a skill alone certifies it only for the tracker that ran it and the state it started from, whereas a sequence keeps one tracker and starts each skill wherever the last one ended. Prior work meets these two conditions mostly by training; CHOREO restores them without retraining by treating every skill as a trajectory that any tracker can run. It assigns each instruction the most precise of its best-validated frozen trackers, which ends each skill closer to the next one's start. It then builds each transition from the measured robot state, escalating to bridges and standing only when needed. On 400 instructions, CHOREO lifts sequence success to 95.8\% and beats always standing between skills by 2.8 points with 42\% shorter transitions. On a physical Unitree G1, all 45 zero-shot trials of nine five-action instructions succeed.

signals.title: Connectivity-Aware Exploration of Robotic Grasp Spaces
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.22983v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robotic grasping is typically formulated as the problem of identifying successful actions from a space of candidate grasp poses. However, the organization of successful actions within this space has received less attention. We study the multiscale structure of viable robotic grasps in SE(3) and investigate whether this structure can be exploited for more efficient exploration. Using a large-scale grasp dataset, we show that successful grasp sets exhibit heterogeneous and reproducible connectivity structure across objects. We then introduce a connectivity-aware sampling strategy that incrementally explores the currently observed grasp space by prioritizing potential bridges between components, structural frontiers, boundary extensions, and geometric novelty. In controlled reconstruction experiments, the method recovers the connectivity structure of successful grasp sets substantially more efficiently than random sampling and farthest-point sampling. We further evaluate whether connectivity acquired under hidden grasp viability can improve subsequent grasp discovery, and whether structural experience from previously explored objects can be retrieved and transferred to unseen objects. These results suggest that the spatial organization of viable actions provides information relevant to grasp-space exploration beyond the viability of individual candidate actions. More broadly, they motivate structure-aware exploration as a means of exploiting the geometry of viable action spaces in robotic manipulation.

signals.title: NEXUS: Perceptive Whole-Body Control for Terrain-Adaptive Teleoperation
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.39000v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whole-body teleoperation requires a humanoid robot to reproduce a human operator's behavior even when their terrains differ. This demands that the robot perceive local terrain and adapt its posture and contacts accordingly, rather than copy the operator's motion frame by frame. However, paired motion data linking the same behaviors across flat ground and different terrains remain scarce, limiting supervision for learning terrain-adaptive control. To enable whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains, we introduce NEXUS, a perceptive whole-body control framework that combines human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback. We first develop a scalable terrain-aware adaptation algorithm that efficiently generates high-quality motion pairs across motions and terrains without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using a paired motion corpus totaling nearly 1,000 hours, we train a perceptive whole-body controller through teacher-student learning to reproduce commanded behaviors across terrains. Experiments demonstrate efficient, scalable generation of high-quality motion data and show that NEXUS combines broad behavioral coverage with terrain adaptability and tracking fidelity, outperforming existing whole-body controllers on the evaluated benchmarks. Zero-shot real-world deployment enables real-time whole-body teleoperation on diverse unseen terrains, further validating the generalization of our method. Project website: https://nexus-humanoid.github.io/

signals.title: Visual Foresight for Agentic Reasoning Before Action in Urban Navigation
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.04916v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of action consequences, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, a training-free agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with visual foresight for reasoning before action. Our central idea is to use predicted future views to assess proposed actions in the context of persistent medium-horizon subgoals and observed experience. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. To enable visual foresight, a predictive world sandbox uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to generate future views of proposed movements, providing visual cues for reasoning about their consequences beyond the current observation. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions using the subgoal and accumulated experience to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

signals.title: From Language to Motion: Task-Conditioned Focal-Stack Trajectory Integration for Microscopic Robots
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.12241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Microscopic visual servoing requires a robot to follow fine geometric features that a single image may reveal only in part. At high magnification, the field of view is limited, and shallow depth of field can leave different sections of the same contour sharp at different focal settings. These constraints also make training data costly to annotate, particularly when a change in part or task calls for a different edge, boundary, or offset path. We present a language-guided framework that addresses both the cost of configuring new tasks and the loss of usable geometry in any single focal plane. A language instruction specifies the geometry to recover, while frozen perception models and geometric operators locate it in the images. This separation enables zero-shot reconfiguration for the evaluated tasks without new task-specific training labels. To recover a path across focal planes, we extract local trajectories first and then select a consistent path from the segments supported by the image evidence. Each focal plane can thus contribute the sections it resolves well. The evaluated configuration took 15 minutes. Across nine part and illumination conditions, trajectory-level integration reduced 2-D contour RMSE by 56.4% relative to image-first fusion with SAMFF. In robot dispensing experiments, target-region coverage increased from 83.5% to 92.9%.

signals.title: LiteNWM: Efficient Latent World Models for Onboard Visual Navigation in the Wild
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.12368v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Direct visual navigation policies generate trajectories efficiently but do not explicitly evaluate their future consequences. Generative navigation world models provide this foresight through visual rollouts, which are costly when evaluating multiple candidates. We present LiteNWM, a latent navigation world model that shares visual encoding across candidates and jointly predicts their action-conditioned future representations at multiple horizons, while a learned scorer uses these predictions to select trajectories. In offline evaluations on RECON, SCAND, and SACSoN, LiteNWM reduces macro-averaged trajectory error by 17.56% relative to NoMaD+NWM-XL and achieves a 128.00-fold end-to-end speedup on an RTX 5090. The same evaluator transfers from NoMaD to MBRA without proposer-specific retraining, reducing MBRA's macro-averaged trajectory error by 16.2%. In real-robot experiments in unseen indoor and outdoor environments, LiteNWM improves navigation success from 43.3% to 83.3% relative to NoMaD. These results demonstrate that LiteNWM can be deployed for future-aware planning and closed-loop navigation on a physical robot.

signals.title: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.21522v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.

signals.title: Safe Task Completion via Graph-Based Planning for LLM-Powered Robots
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.24603v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are used to drive robotic manipulation and planning, yet deploying them on physical systems exposes risks, including jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mostly evaluated on short instructions with a single hazard. Real tasks may mix safe and unsafe sub-tasks, or combine individually safe actions into an unsafe outcome. For such compound instructions, a single safety decision either misses the hazard or rejects the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-powered robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules framework that verifies safety at multiple stages rather than relying on a single one. Five agents ground safety principles into world-specific rules, judge each sub-task in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is organized as a graph in which each node handles its assigned rules. Candidate plans are verified and aggregated level by level until one plan satisfies every rule. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions from two benchmarks, measuring Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reaches 0% ASR on both benchmarks and highest TSR among all methods, with 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 83.51% on our long-horizon compound instructions.

signals.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.25600v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.

signals.title: From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.28164v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.

signals.title: MyoAcross: A Framework for Scalable Individualized Musculoskeletal Simulation with a Generalist Morphology-Conditioned Policy
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.36535v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Musculoskeletal simulations powered by deep reinforcement learning (DRL) support human-robot interaction design and rehabilitation engineering, and they typically rely on a generic template model. However, differences in skeletal proportions and body mass alter dynamics, limiting the fidelity of generic models and the reuse of policies trained on them. Scaling individualized simulations requires a framework that connects model construction from accessible inputs with a generalist policy that transfers without fine-tuning. We present MyoAcross, which integrates skeletal-guided individual model construction, generalist morphology-conditioned policy learning, and virtual model augmentation for full-body muscle-driven control. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion with a 53.70 mm tracking error, compared with 8.32% completion for a baseline policy trained only on the generic model. Ablation studies show that morphology conditioning improves tracking accuracy while virtual model augmentation broadens generalization. Across input modalities, the pretrained policy demonstrates generalizability to models constructed from body shape (paired with mass), monocular images (paired with height and mass), and marker-based motion capture (paired with mass), making MyoAcross scalable. For biomechanical assessment, MyoAcross improves agreement with measured ground reaction forces and surface electromyography over the generic model on the external Gait120 dataset. These results establish MyoAcross as a practical framework for scalable individualized musculoskeletal simulation. It is suited for systematic cross-individual applications, such as exoskeleton DRL assistance policy design.

signals.title: A Bi-level Co-design Framework for Lunar Monoped with 2D Jump and Landing Control
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.37199v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Legged robots for lunar exploration must be designed for low gravity, where reduced contact forces and long flight phases make leg morphology and controller choice interdependent. We study this for a planar monoped in lunar gravity (1.625 m/s^2) using a bi-level co-design framework: a differential evolution outer loop searches over link lengths, and each candidate is evaluated on a vertical jump by either a quadratic program based task-space controller (QP-TSC) or a direct-collocation based trajectory optimization. The two controllers yield different optimal link lengths, and trajectory optimization outperforms the QP-TSC across most of the design space, with 17% lower Cost of Transport (COT) at their respective optima. We then extend to a 2D jump, where trajectory optimization with centroidal angular momentum regulation produces stable in-place and forward jumps, and an LQR controller absorbs impact and stabilizes the robot after touchdown. This is demonstrated on a baseline morphology with both links 0.3 m long.

signals.title: When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.41857v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulation benchmarks score robot policies by success rate, and every failed episode counts against the policy. Testing over ten vision language action and world action models on five benchmarks, we find that failures in which the policy has placed the object and the simulator then throws it out are frequent, and that the benchmark's own scripted demonstrations fail the same way. We present SimuGuard, an auditing plugin for LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa, RoboDojo and RoboLab. At every physics step, it records the state and flags an object that starts moving at a contact faster than the robot's contact or gravity account for. It replays a recorded episode bit for bit, and it reruns the episode with one solver parameter changed. With it we trace each such episode to a false contact. A fixed threshold in PhysX's collision detection makes the engine report an overlap of about two centimeters between the placed object and the thin wall of its container, where the two do not touch. The solver removes the whole overlap in one step and throws the object out at several meters per second. With a smaller threshold, LingBot-VA succeeds in 98 of 100 new episodes against 89, and no episode has an artifact. Across five models, the ranking in the repaired engine follows the ranking on a real robot. SimuGuard also finds two other simulation errors: objects that start inside their support, and objects stuck to an open gripper. SimuGuard lets a benchmark separate what the policy did from what the solver did.

signals.title: Positive Safety Margins from Artificial Potential Field Reward Augmentation for Size-Robust Obstacle Avoidance under Partial Observability
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.02947v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Collision-free reaching is central to manipulation, yet real cells often leave the size and exact position of an obstacle unobserved, which excludes reinforcement learning controllers that take obstacle geometry as input. A reward limited to a collision penalty does not depend on the clearance outside the obstacle, so under a step cost its learned policy skims the obstacle surface and fails once the obstacle radius exceeds its training value. We investigate whether a single analytic reward term can induce a safety margin without exposing the obstacle to the policy. We augment the reward of a simulated Franka Emika Panda reaching task with a horizontal artificial potential field that penalizes proximity within a safety margin around each of two pillars (fixed nominal layout, random drift). Under hidden observation, policies trained with this term maintain a safe success rate above 88% across a radius sweep from 0.03 m to 0.055 m (30 seeds), while policies without it fall below 10% at the maximum tested radius; the term induces a minimum clearance of 47.9 mm against 9.6 mm without it and eliminates training collisions at least eight times earlier (median steps). The advantage is statistically significant at all out-of-distribution radii and holds across three reinforcement learning solvers and under full observation. Its safe success rate is comparable to that of a classical potential-field planner given the pillar positions. The margin is a fixed buffer rather than an adaptation to the radius, and it lengthens the path by about 19%.

signals.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.03850v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating embodied-AI policies in closed loop across simulation benchmarks such as LIBERO and RoboTwin requires repeated integration, as each benchmark defines its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention. Evaluation can also be slow: with a StarVLA checkpoint, the 5,000 episodes of RoboTwin Easy take 17.5 hours on four RTX PRO 5000 GPUs. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluators identifies two bottlenecks: alternating between one simulator and inference leaves the GPU at only 14.3% average utilization on LIBERO-Long, while rendering at every control step on RoboTwin means an action-chunk policy reads only one of every 16 rendered observations. We present RoboScope Kit, an evaluation toolkit that integrates each model and benchmark once through a unified interface, keeping each benchmark's native evaluator and scoring, and accelerates evaluation through two mechanisms. (1) Scheduling: simulator workers and policy replicas scale independently, with autotuning sizing both pools to each workload and host. (2) Runtime optimization: the simulation runtime skips unconsumed simulation and rendering work without changing the policy's inputs or outcomes. On a single RTX 4090, RoboScope Kit runs LIBERO-Long 6.2$\times$ faster and 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes 13.2$\times$ faster than StarVLA, and 2.1-7.3$\times$ faster than RLinf and vla-eval. Scaling to four RTX PRO 5000 GPUs, it evaluates all 5,000 RoboTwin Easy episodes in 66 minutes (15.8$\times$ faster). LIBERO-Long success rates stay within 0.3 percentage points of StarVLA, and every RoboTwin episode matches its exact outcome and terminal step.

signals.title: CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.03932v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Feature matching underpins many robotic perception tasks, including visual localization, mapping, SLAM, and autonomous navigation. Existing semi-dense matchers predict confidence on fixed grids, limiting correspondences to predefined locations and requiring costly high-resolution grids for precise localization. We present CoReMatch (Coordinate Refinement Match), a recurrent framework that refines correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space rather than predicting discrete confidence maps. CoReMatch progressively improves correspondence estimates by propagating information across iterations. At the coarse stage, a Deep Aggregated Transformer captures global context and iteratively updates correspondence coordinates, while a lightweight regression head further sharpens their localization. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show that CoReMatch strikes a strong balance between accuracy and efficiency, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running more than 10x faster on embedded edge hardware. These results demonstrate that recurrent coordinate refinement offers an efficient and scalable approach to real-time feature matching for robotic perception.

signals.title: RoboARCade: Benchmarking Agentic Robot Control
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.08209v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.

signals.title: GraSLA: A Lightweight Spatial-Language-Action Model with Grasp Hypotheses as Geometric Priors
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.15659v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper focuses on improving the precision and adaptability of language-conditioned manipulation policies learned through imitation learning. Recently, action-based methods have become mainstream for closed-loop control, yet implicit behavior learning from demonstrations limits their generalization beyond training conditions. To address this, explicit geometric priors offer direct guidance for action prediction. In particular, 6-DoF grasp detection generates diverse grasp hypotheses with explicit approach directions for the gripper. Yet raw hypotheses span multiple regions and lack task semantics, requiring joint reasoning with the scene and instruction. To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as explicit geometric priors. Specifically, it encodes multi-view point clouds, the instruction, and grasp hypotheses, binds task-relevant ones to scene context and task semantics via bidirectional cross-attention, and decodes continuous action chunks. Experiments show that, with 0.29B parameters, 39.5 ms latency, and no robot-data pretraining, GraSLA outperforms existing baselines, achieving 99.3% on LIBERO, 73.7% on LIBERO+, and 53.33% on LIBERO-Pro.

signals.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.16246v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models drive the robot directly from camera views, yet a VLA alone shows three typical failures. It walks past the goal, stops before reaching it, and rarely recovers after going off track. Pairing a VLA with a large language model (LLM) planner fixes these failures, but queries the LLM throughout every episode, adding token costs and latency. We introduce Harness-to-Executor (H2E), a task-level distillation method that pairs an LLM planner and a frozen VLA as a heterogeneous training agent, keeps only sessions that reach the goal, and then trains a VLA alone on them so no LLM is used at test time. In these sessions, the planner gives sub-instructions and moves the robot with its own tools, detours are common, and the planner decides when to stop. H2E therefore labels every motion as a VLA action for the original task, whoever made it. It masks the loss on steps moving away from the goal and assigns end labels to states near it, so the VLA learns where the task ends. H2E sets a new state of the art on REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE. It raises an 8B VLA's success rate by 15.6% and 11.1% respectively, surpassing a method trained on 10M samples. The distilled VLA exceeds its agent on unseen episodes with zero LLM tokens and runs 3.7 times faster.

signals.title: STVLA: Spatial-aware and Temporal-memory forVision-Language-Action Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.16589v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $\pi_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{https://stvla.github.io/}{https://stvla.github.io/}

signals.title: Rethinking Actions: Continuity-Aware Priors for World-Model Planning
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.16645v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal. Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with the GP residual using expert future actions. The resulting planner achieves 87.07\% macro success across five simulated tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with 71.03\% for INTACT, 61.66\% for PRISM, and 58.66\% for LeWM. Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.

signals.title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.20402v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Koopman operator theory lets linear controllers handle nonlinear robots: an encoder lifts the state into a latent space with approximately linear dynamics, on which LQR or MPC is designed. A controller that stabilizes the latent model, however, may fail to stabilize the real nonlinear system. Stability is analyzed on latent rollouts, where the linear model propagates its own predictions, but on the robot the nonlinear dynamics produce each next state, which the controller re-encodes at every step. We prove that latent stability transfers to the robot when the latent model reproduces the true closed-loop dynamics to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We also derive a margin for approximate matching and show that an open-loop stable latent model cannot match the plant's linearization at an unstable equilibrium. We propose Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and builds first-order matching to it into the Koopman matrices. At the target, TIK's feedback gain equals the LQR gain of this linearization, and a bilinear input term models state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. On four simulated open-loop unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers stabilize their latent models but are locally unstable on the real system, whereas all 40 TIK controllers stabilize it. An offline stability test with empirical curvature estimates identifies the stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems but is inconclusive under high noise. Given explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction under local feedback after entry. TIK reaches 88% success in constrained cart-pole swi

signals.title: ReuseMem: One Memory, Multiple Goals in Robot Manipulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.21115v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes. Project Page: https://yoondol.github.io/reusemem/

signals.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.22356v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.

signals.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.22543v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In

signals.title: RecallFlow: Episodic Memory as the Source Distribution of Generative Robot Policies
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23731v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.

signals.title: PartSLAM: Unsupervised Part-based Scene Modeling for Fast Succinct Map Matching
signals.summary: arXiv:2306.10782v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we explore the challenging 1-to-N map matching problem, which exploits a compact description of map data, to improve the scalability of map matching techniques used by various robot vision tasks. We propose a first method explicitly aimed at fast succinct map matching, which consists only of map-matching subtasks. These tasks include offline map matching attempts to find a compact part-based scene model that effectively explains each map using fewer larger parts. The tasks also include an online map matching attempt to efficiently find correspondence between the part-based maps. Our part-based scene modeling approach is unsupervised and uses common pattern discovery (CPD) between the input and known reference maps. This enables a robot to learn a compact map model without human intervention. We also present a practical implementation that uses the state-of-the-art CPD technique of randomized visual phrases (RVP) with a compact bounding box (BB) based part descriptor, which consists of keypoint and descriptor BBs. The results of our challenging map-matching experiments, which use a publicly available radish dataset, show that the proposed approach achieves successful map matching with significant speedup and a compact description of map data that is tens of times more compact. Although this paper focuses on the standard 2D point-set map and the BB-based part representation, we believe our approach is sufficiently general to be applicable to a broad range of map formats, such as the 3D point cloud map, as well as to general bounding volumes and other compact part representations.

signals.title: SegSTRONG-C: Segmenting Surgical Tools Robustly On Non-adversarial Generated Corruptions -- An EndoVis'24 Challenge
signals.summary: arXiv:2407.11906v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Surgical data science has seen rapid advancement with the excellent performance of end-to-end deep neural networks (DNNs). Despite their successes, DNNs have been proven susceptible to minor ``corruptions,'' substantially impairing the model's performance, introducing a major concern for the translation of cutting-edge technology, especially in high-stakes scenarios. We introduce the SegSTRONG-C challenge dedicated to better understanding model deterioration under unforeseen but plausible non-adversarial ``corruption'' and the capabilities of contemporary methods that seek to improve it. Built on a dataset generated through counterfactual robotic replay, SegSTRONG-C provides paired clean and ``corrupted'' samples, enabling reproducible evaluation of model robustness. Participants are challenged to train tool segmentation algorithms on ``uncorrupted'' data and evaluate them on ``corrupted'' test domains for the binary robot tool segmentation task. Through comprehensive baseline experiments and participating submissions from widespread community engagement, SegSTRONG-C reveals key themes for model failure and identifies promising directions for improving robustness. The challenge winners achieved an average of 0.9394 DSC and 0.9301 NSD across the unreleased test sets with ``corruption'' types: bleeding, smoke, and low brightness. This highlights how prior knowledge, customized training strategies, and architectural choice can be leveraged to improve robustness. In conclusion, the SegSTRONG-C challenge has identified practical approaches for enhancing model robustness. However, most approaches rely on conventional techniques that have known limitations. Looking ahead, we advocate for expanding intellectual diversity

signals.title: RaCalNet: Radar Calibration Network for Sparse-Supervised Metric Depth Estimation
signals.summary: arXiv:2506.15560v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dense depth estimation using millimeter-wave radar typically requires dense LiDAR supervision, generated via multi-frame projection and interpolation, for guiding the learning of accurate depth from sparse radar measurements and RGB images. However, this paradigm is both costly and data-intensive. To address this, we propose RaCalNet, a novel framework that eliminates the need for dense supervision by using sparse LiDAR to supervise the learning of refined radar measurements, resulting in a supervision density of merely around 1\% compared to dense-supervised methods. RaCalNet is composed of two key modules. The Radar Recalibration module performs radar point screening and pixel-wise displacement refinement, producing accurate and reliable depth priors from sparse radar inputs. These priors are then used by the Metric Depth Optimization module, which learns to infer scene-level scale priors and fuses them with monocular depth predictions to achieve metrically accurate outputs. This modular design enhances structural consistency and preserves fine-grained geometric details. Despite relying solely on sparse supervision, RaCalNet produces depth maps with clear object contours and fine-grained textures, demonstrating superior visual quality compared to state-of-the-art dense-supervised methods. Quantitatively, it achieves performance comparable to existing methods on the ZJU-4DRadarCam dataset and yields a 34.89\% RMSE reduction in real-world deployment scenarios. We plan to gradually release the code and models in the future at https://github.com/818slam/RaCalNet.git.

signals.title: U-ViLAR: Uncertainty-Aware Visual Localization for Autonomous Driving via Differentiable Association and Registration
signals.summary: arXiv:2507.04503v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate localization using visual information is a critical yet challenging task, especially in urban environments where nearby buildings and construction sites significantly degrade GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) signal quality. This issue underscores the importance of visual localization techniques in scenarios where GNSS signals are unreliable. This paper proposes U-ViLAR, a novel uncertainty-aware visual localization framework designed to address these challenges while enabling adaptive localization using high-definition (HD) maps or navigation maps. Specifically, our method first extracts features from the input visual data and maps them into Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) space to enhance spatial consistency with the map input. Subsequently, we introduce: a) Perceptual Uncertainty-guided Association, which mitigates errors caused by perception uncertainty, and b) Localization Uncertainty-guided Registration, which reduces errors introduced by localization uncertainty. By effectively balancing the coarse-grained large-scale localization capability of association with the fine-grained precise localization capability of registration, our approach achieves robust and accurate localization. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple localization tasks. Furthermore, our model has undergone rigorous testing on large-scale autonomous driving fleets and has demonstrated stable performance in various challenging urban scenarios.

signals.title: Prescribed Time Higher Order Control Lyapunov-Barrier Functions
signals.summary: arXiv:2507.13888v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a framework based on Repeated-Root Prescribed Time Higher-Order Control Lyapunov- Barrier Functions (RR-Pxt-HOCL-BF) that guarantees convergence to a safe set/ goal set within user-specified time. Unlike conventional Higher-Order Control Barrier Functions, which does not provide any guarantee on reaching the safe set if the system is initially not in safe set, the proposed method enforces convergence within a prescribed time horizon. This is achieved through a structured differential constraint derived from repeated roots of the characteristic polynomial, leading to closed-form polynomial solutions that ensure convergence at the desired time. Analytical conditions for forward invariance and prescribed-time reachability are derived, with explicit formulations for second-order systems. The approach is validated on an acceleration-controlled unicycle and an inverted pendulum and compared with existing HOCBF methods. Simulation results demonstrate reliable convergence within the desired time horizon, even in scenarios where conventional approaches fail.

signals.title: To New Beginnings: A Survey of Unified Perception in Autonomous Vehicle Software
signals.summary: arXiv:2508.20892v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous vehicle perception typically relies on modular pipelines that decompose the task into detection, tracking, and prediction. While interpretable, these pipelines suffer from error accumulation and limited inter-task synergy.
